title: Diabetes Tests: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Diabetes , also known as diabetes mellitus, is a disease that affects how your body uses glucose ( blood sugar ). Glucose is your body's main source of energy. A hormone Â (a chemical messenger in your bloodstream that controls the actions of certain cells or organs) called insulin helps move glucose from your bloodstream into your cells.

title: Diabetes Tests: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: If you have diabetes, your body can't make insulin or can't use it as well as it should, or both. Too much glucose stays in your blood and doesn't reach your cells. This can cause glucose levels to get too high , which can lead to serious health conditions . These may include heart disease , nerve damage , eye problems , and kidney disease .

title: Diabetes Tests: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Your blood glucose can also drop below what is healthy for you . If it drops very low, you could lose consciousness or have a seizure .

title: Diabetes Tests: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Diabetes tests most often measure glucose levels in your blood to monitor your blood glucose level or see if you have or are at risk for diabetes. Urine tests for diabetes are not used as much since they are not as accurate, and you would need a blood test to diagnose diabetes.

title: Diabetes Tests: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Other names: blood glucose, fasting plasma glucose, FPG, oral glucose tolerance test, OGTT, glucose screening test, glucose in urine test, hemoglobin A1c, random blood sugar, blood sugar, fasting blood sugar (FBS)

title: Blood Glucose | Blood Sugar | MedlinePlus
text: Blood glucose, or blood sugar, is the main sugar found in your blood. It is your body's primary source of energy. It comes from the food you eat. Your body breaks down most of that food into glucose and releases it into your bloodstream. When your blood glucose goes up, it signals your pancreas to release insulin. Insulin is a hormone that helps the glucose get into your cells to be used for energy.

title: Blood Glucose | Blood Sugar | MedlinePlus
text: Diabetes is a disease in which your blood glucose levels are too high. When you have diabetes, your body doesn't make enough insulin, can't use it as well as it should, or both. Too much glucose stays in your blood and doesn't reach your cells. Over time, having too much glucose in your blood can cause serious health problems (diabetes complications). So if you have diabetes, it's important to keep your blood glucose levels within your target range.

title: Blood Glucose | Blood Sugar | MedlinePlus
text: If you have diabetes, your blood glucose target is the range you try to reach as much as possible. The typical targets are:

title: Blood Glucose | Blood Sugar | MedlinePlus
text: Your blood glucose targets may be different, depending on your age, any additional health problems you have, and other factors. Talk with your health care team  about the best target range for you.

title: Blood Glucose | Blood Sugar | MedlinePlus
text: If you have diabetes, you'll likely need to check your blood glucose every day to make sure that your blood glucose numbers are in your target range. Some people may need to check their blood glucose several times a day. Ask your health care team how often you need to check it.

title: Blood Glucose | Blood Sugar | MedlinePlus
text: The most common way to check your blood glucose level at home is with a blood glucose meter. A blood glucose meter measures the amount of glucose in a small sample of blood, usually from your fingertip.

title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know: MedlinePlus
text: Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some cholesterol to work properly. But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk of coronary artery disease and other heart diseases .

title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know: MedlinePlus
text: A blood test called a lipoprotein or lipid panel can measure your cholesterol levels. Before the test, you'll usually need to fast (not eat or drink anything but water) for 9 to 12 hours. Follow the instructions your health care provider gives you.

title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know: MedlinePlus
text: Cholesterol numbers are measured in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL). Talk with your provider about what your cholesterol numbers should be. The numbers that are best for you may depend on your age, race, blood pressure, weight, family history, and more. title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know: MedlinePlus
text: Triglycerides are not a type of cholesterol, but they are also measured in this test.  A normal triglyceride level is below 150 mg/dL. You might need treatment if you have triglyceride levels that are borderline high (150-199 mg/dL) or high (200 mg/dL or more).

title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know: MedlinePlus
text: If you have heart disease, or your provider thinks you might be at higher risk, they may use your LDL cholesterol level to help you set goals for your LDL cholesterol levels.

title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know: MedlinePlus
text: Your provider may use a new risk estimator tool called PREVENT, which stands for Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs, to guide these goals and estimate your risk of heart disease. It looks at factors like your age, health history, and family history, and puts you in a risk group.

title: Autoantibody Testing: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Autoantibody testing checks a sample of your blood for autoantibodies, proteins made by the immune system .

title: Autoantibody Testing: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Normally, your immune system makes proteins called antibodies to attack germs that could make you sick. Autoantibodies, however, do not attack germs. They instead attack your own healthy tissue and organs, believing them to be foreign substances. This can lead to the development of an autoimmune disease. There are more than 80 types of autoimmune diseases , and they can affect almost any part of your body.

title: C-Peptide Test: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: This test measures the level of C-peptide in a sample of your blood or urine (pee). C-peptide is a chain of amino acids (the building blocks of proteins) that your pancreas makes in the process of making insulin. Insulin is a hormone that your pancreas makes to help blood glucose Â (blood sugar) get into your cells, where it can be used for energy. This helps keep your blood glucose at healthy levels.

title: C-Peptide Test: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: C-peptide and insulin enter your bloodstream at the same time and in equal amounts, but C-peptide stays in your blood longer. It is also unaffected by outside sources of insulin such as the medicines involved in diabetes Â treatment. In other words, C-peptide can give an accurate picture of how much insulin your body is making naturally.

title: C-Peptide Test: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Because of this, health care providers may rely on a C-peptide test to measure insulin levels rather than testing insulin levels directly.

title: C-Peptide Test: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: You may need a C-peptide test if you have been diagnosed with a pancreatic tumor (insulinoma) or hypoglycemia (low blood glucose) without a clear cause.

title: C-Peptide Test: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: A C-peptide test usually uses a sample of your blood. But the test may also be done on a sample of all your urine collected over a 24-hour period.

title: Gestational DiabetesÂ |  MedlinePlus
text: If you have diabetes , your blood glucose , or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose comes from the foods you eat. A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells to give them energy. With type 1 diabetes , your body does not make insulin. With type 2 diabetes , your body does not make or use insulin well. Without enough insulin, the glucose stays in your blood.

title: Gestational DiabetesÂ |  MedlinePlus
text: Some people already have diabetes before they get pregnant. But others may develop diabetes during pregnancy. This type of diabetes is called gestational diabetes. It usually develops around the 24th week of pregnancy. It happens when your body can't make the extra insulin it needs during pregnancy. Researchers think gestational diabetes is caused by the hormonal changes of pregnancy, along with genetic and lifestyle factors.

title: Gestational DiabetesÂ |  MedlinePlus
text: Anyone who is pregnant could develop gestational diabetes. But you are more likely to develop it if you:

title: Gestational DiabetesÂ |  MedlinePlus
text: Gestational diabetes often has no symptoms. If you do have symptoms, they may be mild, such as being thirstier than normal or having to urinate (pee) more often.

title: Gestational DiabetesÂ |  MedlinePlus
text: If you are pregnant, you will most likely be screened for gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. But if you have an increased chance of developing gestational diabetes, you may be tested during your first prenatal visit . Your health care provider will use one or more blood glucose tests to check for gestational diabetes. You may have the glucose challenge test, the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or both.

title: Gestational DiabetesÂ |  MedlinePlus
text: For these two tests, you will drink a sugary liquid and wait for an hour before your blood sample is taken. If you have an oral glucose tolerance test, you will also get your blood drawn after 2 and 3 hours.

title: Ketones in Blood: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: A ketones in blood test measures the level of ketones in your blood. Ketones are acids that your body makes when it breaks down fat for energy.

title: Ketones in Blood: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: Normally, the cells in your body use blood glucose , also called blood sugar, for energy. You get glucose from foods you eat, such as carbohydrates . Your body breaks down most of that food into glucose and releases it into your bloodstream. If your cells can't get enough glucose, your body will break down fat for energy instead. This process produces an acid called ketones. If your body breaks down fat too fast, ketones can build up in your blood and urine.

title: Ketones in Blood: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: High ketone levels make your blood too acidic. This is a serious condition called ketoacidosis. The most common type of ketoacidosis is a c omplication of diabetes called diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA is a medical emergency that often develops quickly and can lead to a coma and be life-threatening.

title: Ketones in Blood: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: If you have diabetes, a ketones in blood test can help find high ketone levels early so you can get treatment right away. If your health care provider recommends frequent testing to check for increasing ketone levels, at-home blood testing meters are available that check both glucose levels and ketones. At-home testing for ketones in urine Â testing may also be an option. Talk with your provider about which is right for you.

title: Ketones in Blood: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: A ketones in blood test is mostly used to check for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in people with diabetes. DKA can affect anyone with diabetes, but it is most common with type 1 diabetes . With t ype 2 diabetes , DKA is less common.

title: Ketones in Blood: MedlinePlus Medical Test
text: If you have diabetes, a blood ketones test may be used when you are sick or pregnant. You may also be tested if you develop diabetes during pregnancy .

title: Diabetes
text: In 2022 , 14% of adults aged 18 years and older were living with diabetes, an increase from 7% in 1990. More than half (59%) of adults aged 30 years and over living with diabetes were not taking medication for their diabetes in 2022. Diabetes treatment coverage was lowest in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Diabetes
text: In 2023, diabetes was the direct cause of 2.0 million deaths and 44% of all deaths due to diabetes occurred before the age of 70 years. Another 390 000 kidney disease deaths were caused by diabetes, and high blood glucose causes around 10% of cardiovascular deaths (1) .

title: Diabetes
text: Since 2000, mortality rates from diabetes have been increasing. By contrast, the probability of dying from any one of the four main noncommunicable diseases (cardiovascular diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases or diabetes) between the ages of 30 and 70 decreased by 21% globally between 2000 and 2023.

title: Diabetes
text: Symptoms of diabetes may occur suddenly. In type 2 diabetes, the symptoms can be mild and may take many years to be noticed.

title: Diabetes
text: People with diabetes have a higher risk of health problems including heart attack, stroke and kidney failure.

title: Diabetes
text: Many people with diabetes develop problems with their feet from nerve damage and poor blood flow. This can cause foot ulcers and may lead to amputation.

title: Diabetes
text: Type 1 diabetes (previously known as insulin-dependent, juvenile or childhood-onset) is characterized by deficient insulin production and requires daily administration of insulin. In 2017 there were 9 million people with type 1 diabetes; the majority of them live in high-income countries. Neither its cause nor the means to prevent it are known.

title: Diabetes
text: Type 2 diabetes affects how your body uses sugar (glucose) for energy. It stops the body from using insulin properly, which can lead to high levels of blood sugar if not treated.

title: CDC - What is Diabetes Basics
text: Diabetes is a chronic (long-lasting) health condition that affects how your body turns food into energy. Your body breaks down most of the food you eat into sugar (glucose) and releases it into your bloodstream. When your blood sugar goes up, it signals your pancreas to release insulin. Insulin acts like a key to let the blood sugar into your body’s cells for use as energy. With diabetes, your body doesn’t make enough insulin or can’t use it as well as it should. There are three main types: type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes.

title: CDC - Type 1 Diabetes Causes and Management
text: If you have type 1 diabetes, your body produces very little or no insulin. This occurs because the body's immune system attacks and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas by mistake. This condition is usually diagnosed in children, teens, and young adults, but it can develop at any age. Symptoms often develop quickly, over a few weeks or months. Currently, no one knows how to prevent type 1 diabetes. People with type 1 diabetes must take insulin injections or use an insulin pump every day to survive and manage their blood glucose levels.

title: CDC - Type 2 Diabetes Overview
text: Type 2 diabetes affects how your body uses sugar (glucose) for energy. It stops the body from using insulin properly (insulin resistance), leading to elevated blood sugar levels. Most people with diabetes have type 2. You are at higher risk if you are overweight or obese, are 45 years or older, have a family history of diabetes, or are active less than 3 times a week. It can be prevented or delayed with lifestyle measures including healthy eating, weight loss, and physical activity.

title: CDC - Diabetes Signs, Symptoms & Patient Manifestations
section: Cardinal Symptoms and Patient Clinical Presentation
text: Classic clinical signs and symptoms of diabetes mellitus: 1. Excessive Thirst (Polydipsia): Feeling thirsty all the time, unquenchable thirst, or dry mouth even after drinking plenty of water. This occurs because high blood glucose draws water out of body tissues, causing cellular dehydration and signaling the brain's thirst center. 2. Frequent Urination (Polyuria): Needing to urinate frequently, especially getting up multiple times at night (nocturia). When blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (~180 mg/dL), excess sugar spills into urine, drawing large volumes of water with it via osmotic diuresis. 3. Extreme Hunger (Polyphagia): Constant hunger even while eating, because glucose cannot enter cells without sufficient insulin action. 4. Unexplained Weight Loss: Despite eating normally, the body breaks down muscle and fat for fuel due to lack of intracellular glucose. 5. Chronic Fatigue and Weakness: Feeling exhausted because cells are deprived of energy. 6. Blurry Vision: High blood sugar pulls fluid from the lenses of the eyes, impairing focusing ability. 7. Slow-Healing Sores and Frequent Infections: Impaired circulation and compromised white blood cell function.

title: ADA Clinical Criteria - Fasting, Postprandial & Prediabetes Diagnostics
text: American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes: 1. Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG): Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) between 100 and 125 mg/dL (5.6–6.9 mmol/L). This confirms prediabetes, reflecting hepatic insulin resistance, but does NOT establish a diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes. 2. Postprandial Glucose vs. Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): In healthy individuals, glucose rises after meals and peaks within 1 hour. Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) is strictly defined as a 2-hour plasma glucose between 140 and 199 mg/dL (7.8–11.0 mmol/L) during a standardized 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). A casual or home post-meal glucose reading of ~150 mg/dL cannot independently establish IGT or diabetes because it lacks standardization of carbohydrate load and timing. 3. Diagnostic Confirmation Requirements: A diagnosis of diabetes requires two abnormal test results from the same sample or in two separate test samples (e.g., repeating FPG or pairing with an HbA1c test). Single borderline results do not establish diabetes. 4. Recommended Clinical Next Steps for Prediabetes: Discuss fasting glucose with a primary care provider, obtain a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) test to measure 2- to 3-month glycemic average, consider a formal standardized 2-hour 75g OGTT if recommended by the physician, and initiate lifestyle modifications (structured physical activity of at least 150 minutes/week and Mediterranean/DASH nutritional patterns).

title: ACC/AHA Guidelines - Severe Hypertriglyceridemia & Acute Pancreatitis
text: Clinical Management of Severe Hypertriglyceridemia (ACC/AHA and Endocrine Society Standards): 1. Acute Pancreatitis Risk: A circulating fasting triglyceride level of 1,000 mg/dL or higher (and especially >500 mg/dL) substantially elevates the immediate risk of acute pancreatitis. Normal blood glucose or HbA1c does not mitigate this acute danger. 2. Clinical Action Plan: Immediate, same-day medical assessment is recommended. Clinicians must assess for cardinal symptoms of acute pancreatitis, specifically severe persistent epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. 3. Nutritional & Lifestyle Interventions: For triglycerides >=1,000 mg/dL, standard generic lifestyle advice is inadequate. Current guidance demands a very-low-fat diet (<10% to 15% of total caloric intake from fat) to reduce chylomicron formation, absolute elimination of alcohol, and complete avoidance of added sugars and refined carbohydrates. 4. Investigation of Secondary Etiologies: Clinicians must screen for secondary contributing causes including unmanaged diabetes, hypothyroidism (TSH testing), chronic kidney disease, excessive alcohol intake, medications (estrogens, beta blockers, retinoids), and underlying familial chylomicronemia or genetic lipid disorders. 5. Pharmacotherapy: Guideline-directed medical therapy includes immediate initiation of fibrates (fenofibrate) or high-dose prescription omega-3 fatty acids under medical supervision to rapidly lower triglycerides below the pancreatitis threshold.

title: MedlinePlus - GAD65 Autoantibodies & Islet Cell Testing
section: Autoantibody Testing, GAD65 Biology & C-Peptide Differentiation
text: What is GAD65? Glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65) is an essential intracellular enzyme located inside pancreatic beta cells that catalyzes the conversion of glutamate into gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). In autoimmune diabetes, the immune system mistakenly targets this enzyme, producing circulating GAD65 autoantibodies (GADA / anti-GAD65). Clinical Significance of Positive GAD65: A positive GAD65 antibody result confirms an autoimmune etiology (cause) of diabetes. It is the primary biomarker used by clinicians to identify autoimmune diabetes (Type 1 diabetes and Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults [LADA]) and distinguish them from non-autoimmune Type 2 diabetes (where autoantibodies are negative). Difference Between GAD65 Antibody and C-Peptide Testing: 1. GAD65 Autoantibody tests for CAUSE / ETIOLOGY: It answers 'Is the immune system attacking the pancreas?' 2. C-Peptide tests for FUNCTION / CAPACITY: It measures endogenous insulin secretory reserve, answering 'How much insulin is the pancreas currently producing?' Clinical Comparison: In Type 1 diabetes, GAD65 antibodies are typically positive, while C-peptide is undetectable or very low (<0.2 nmol/L) due to near-total beta-cell destruction. In Type 2 diabetes, GAD65 antibodies are negative, while C-peptide is normal or elevated due to insulin resistance. In LADA (Type 1.5), GAD65 is positive, but C-peptide levels may initially be preserved before progressively declining.

title: MedlinePlus - C-Peptide Test & Endogenous Insulin Secretion
text: A C-peptide test measures endogenous insulin secretion. Proinsulin produced in pancreatic beta cells is cleaved into equimolar amounts of active insulin and connecting peptide (C-peptide). Unlike insulin, C-peptide has a longer half-life, avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism, and is unaffected by exogenous insulin therapy. Clinical Interpretation: 1. In Type 1 diabetes: C-peptide levels are undetectable or profoundly low (<0.2 nmol/L or <0.6 ng/mL), indicating severe/absolute beta-cell failure. 2. In Type 2 diabetes: C-peptide levels are normal or elevated (>0.6 nmol/L), reflecting insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia. 3. In LADA: C-peptide levels are initially preserved or borderline, followed by a steady progressive decline.

title: NIH Bookshelf - Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA)
text: Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), commonly termed Type 1.5 diabetes, is a slow-progressing form of autoimmune diabetes presenting in adulthood. Diagnostic Triad (Immunology of Diabetes Society criteria): 1. Adult age at diagnosis (typically >30 to 35 years). 2. Presence of at least one circulating islet autoantibody (most commonly GADA / anti-GAD65). 3. No insulin requirement for at least the initial 6 months following diagnosis. Clinical Differentiation: Unlike Type 2 diabetes, LADA patients are typically leaner, exhibit progressive beta-cell destruction, and eventually progress to absolute insulin dependence within months to a few years. Unlike acute Type 1 diabetes, beta-cell loss in LADA occurs slowly, allowing temporary glycemic control with diet or oral non-insulin therapies at diagnosis.

title: NIDDK - Monogenic Diabetes and MODY
text: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) is an uncommon form of monogenic diabetes caused by a single gene mutation with autosomal dominant inheritance. Characteristics: onset typically before age 25, absent pancreatic islet autoantibodies, preserved endogenous C-peptide, absence of severe obesity or insulin resistance, and multigenerational family history of diabetes. Common subtypes: MODY 2 (GCK gene mutation causing stable, mild fasting hyperglycemia often requiring no treatment) and MODY 3 (HNF1A gene mutation causing progressive beta-cell dysfunction that responds exquisitely to low-dose sulfonylureas).

title: MedlinePlus - Hypoglycemia Management and Rule of 15
text: Hypoglycemia in diabetes is defined as blood glucose <70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Classification: Level 1 (glucose 54-69 mg/dL), Level 2 (glucose <54 mg/dL / clinically significant), Level 3 (severe hypoglycemia characterized by cognitive impairment requiring external assistance). Symptoms include diaphoresis, tremors, tachycardia, anxiety, neuroglycopenia, confusion, and seizure. Management ('Rule of 15'): Consume 15-20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates (e.g., 4 oz fruit juice, 3-4 glucose tablets), wait 15 minutes, and recheck blood glucose. Repeat until glucose is >=70 mg/dL. For unconscious or severe Level 3 events, administer intramuscular or nasal glucagon.

title: MedlinePlus - Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperglycemic Crises
text: Acute metabolic emergencies of diabetes: 1. Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): Life-threatening complication primarily in Type 1 diabetes, characterized by triad of hyperglycemia (typically >250 mg/dL), high anion gap metabolic acidosis (arterial pH <7.30, serum bicarbonate <18 mEq/L), and hyperketonemia (elevated serum/urine beta-hydroxybutyrate). Driven by absolute insulin deficiency and excess counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol). 2. Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS): Primarily in Type 2 diabetes, characterized by profound hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), severe hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), and severe dehydration, without significant ketoacidosis due to residual endogenous insulin preventing lipolysis.

title: WHO - Long-Term Microvascular and Macrovascular Complications
text: Over time, diabetes can damage the heart, blood vessels, eyes, kidneys, and nerves. Adults with diabetes have a two- to three-fold increased risk of heart attacks and strokes. Diabetic retinopathy is an important cause of blindness, resulting from accumulated damage to small retinal vessels. Neuropathy combined with reduced blood flow increases the risk of foot ulcers, infection, and limb amputation. Diabetes is also among the leading causes of kidney failure (diabetic nephropathy).

title: MedlinePlus - Gestational Diabetes Causes and Risks
text: Gestational diabetes develops during pregnancy in women who did not have diabetes before. Hormones from the placenta cause insulin resistance. Usually diagnosed between the 24th and 28th week of pregnancy, it increases the mother's risk for type 2 diabetes later in life and increases the risk of macrosomia (high birth weight) and cesarean delivery.
